summary: Jesus sets out for Golgotha carrying His cross; soldiers force Simon of Cyrene to carry it after Him, and Jesus warns the weeping women of Jerusalem.
key_insight: Luke says the soldiers laid the cross on Simon “that he might bear it after Jesus.” Jesus had said that whoever does not bear his cross and come after Him cannot be His disciple (Luke 14:27). On the road to Golgotha, a passerby from Cyrene did it in plain sight.
story: When the soldiers had finished mocking Jesus, they took the purple robe off Him, put His own clothes back on Him, and led Him out to crucify Him. Pilate had handed Him over, and Jesus went out “bearing His cross.” {Jn}

As they came out, {Mt} the soldiers laid hold of a man who was coming in from the country, Simon, from the city of Cyrene. {Lk} He was the father of Alexander and Rufus. {Mk} They compelled him to carry the cross, and they laid it on him “that he might bear it after Jesus.” {Lk}

A great multitude of the people followed, among them women who mourned and lamented Him. Jesus turned to them and said, “Daughters of Jerusalem, do not weep for Me, but weep for yourselves and for your children.” {Lk}

The days were coming, He told them, when people would call the childless blessed and would cry to the mountains to fall on them and to the hills to cover them. “For if they do these things in the green wood, what will be done in the dry?” {Lk}
Two others, criminals, were led out with Him to be put to death. {Lk}
differences: John says Jesus went out “bearing His cross” and does not mention Simon. Matthew, Mark and Luke tell of Simon carrying it.
Only Mark names Simon’s sons, Alexander and Rufus. Mark and Luke say he was coming in from the country.
Luke alone says Simon carried the cross “after Jesus,” and alone records the mourning women, Jesus’ words to the daughters of Jerusalem, and the two criminals led out with Him.
Mark says the soldiers took “the purple” off Him; Matthew calls it “the robe.”

fit.question: John says Jesus went out “bearing His cross.” Matthew, Mark and Luke say Simon of Cyrene carried it. Who carried the cross?

points.label: Both, one after the other
points.text: A condemned man normally carried his own cross, usually the crossbeam, to the place of execution. John tells how Jesus set out from Pilate’s headquarters carrying it. Matthew says the soldiers seized Simon “as they came out,” probably as the procession left the city. Jesus began the walk under the cross, and Simon carried it the rest of the way.

points.label: Why Simon was needed
points.text: None of the Gospels says why. Jesus had been scourged and beaten (John 19:1–3), and it is likely He could no longer carry the beam far. Mark’s next words, “they brought Him to the place Golgotha” (15:22), may suggest He needed help even to walk.

points.label: John’s focus
points.text: John stresses that Jesus went to His death of His own will (John 10:18). He does not deny Simon’s part; he simply does not tell it.

fit.note: Each writer tells part of one walk. The accounts complete each other, and none requires an error.
fit.short: Jesus set out carrying His cross (John); on the way the soldiers forced Simon to carry it for Him (Matthew, Mark, Luke).

scene.label: Cyrene
scene.text: Cyrene was a Greek city on the coast of North Africa, in present-day Libya, with a large Jewish community. Jews from Cyrene had a synagogue in Jerusalem (Acts 6:9), and many came up for the feasts (Acts 2:10).

scene.label: Compelled
scene.text: Roman soldiers had the right to press civilians into service to carry loads. Jesus used the same word in the Sermon on the Mount: “whoever compels you to go one mile, go with him two” (Matthew 5:41).

scene.label: Alexander and Rufus
scene.text: Mark names Simon’s sons as if his readers knew them. Paul greets a Rufus in Rome, “chosen in the Lord,” together with his mother (Romans 16:13). Mark probably wrote for believers in Rome, so this may be the same family, though no one can be sure.

scene.label: Outside the city
scene.text: Executions took place outside the city (Leviticus 24:14; Hebrews 13:12), along roads where passersby would see them. Crucifixion was meant as a public warning to anyone who defied Rome.

scene.label: Green wood and dry
scene.text: Green wood does not burn easily; dry wood catches at once. If Rome would do this to Jesus, whom Pilate had called innocent, what would happen to a rebellious city? Jesus’ words about the mountains echo Hosea 10:8. Within forty years Roman armies destroyed Jerusalem.

witnesses.matthew: Matthew moves quickly from the soldiers’ mockery to Golgotha, giving only Simon’s name and city. A man from Cyrene, perhaps a pilgrim come for the feast, is drawn into the death of the King without being asked.
witnesses.mark: Mark names Simon’s sons, Alexander and Rufus, apparently as men his first readers knew. The small detail suggests the family became known in the church, and it shows Mark drawing on people who could vouch for what happened that morning.
witnesses.luke: Luke alone tells of the women of Jerusalem. On the way to His own death Jesus grieves for the city and its children, as He had wept over Jerusalem when He entered it (Luke 19:41–44). Luke also notes the two criminals, so that Jesus goes to the cross “numbered with the transgressors” (Luke 22:37).
witnesses.john: John says only that Jesus went out “bearing His cross.” In John, Jesus lays down His life of His own accord (John 10:18), and John shows Him setting out for Golgotha under His own burden.

seeing.reveals: On the road to His own death, Jesus turned to grieve for others. He did not ask for pity. He warned the women of the judgment coming on their city and their children.
seeing.living: Simon did not choose the cross; it was laid on him, and he carried it behind Jesus. Some burdens come to believers unasked and undeserved. Carried after Jesus, they become part of following Him, and the Gospels remember Simon by name.
seeing.ponder: What cross has been laid on you that you did not choose, and will you carry it after Jesus?

preaching.big_idea: Jesus carried the cross for us, and calls us to carry ours after Him.
outline: A cross laid on a passerby (26)
A warning of judgment to come (29–31)
preaching.watch_for: Luke ties this scene back to Jesus weeping over Jerusalem as He entered it (19:41–44). The women weep for Jesus, but Jesus had wept for the city, and now He tells them to weep for themselves and their children: the true tragedy was Jerusalem’s rejection of its King.
